questions.q: How does machine learning differ from traditional programming?
options: In ML, rules plus data produce answers
In ML, data plus answers produce the rules
ML needs no data, only a clever algorithm
ML programs cannot be run on new data
questions.why: Traditional software applies rules a programmer wrote; ML learns the rules (the model) from examples with known answers. "Rules plus data produce answers" describes the traditional approach, which is why it is the tempting distractor.

questions.q: A finance team asks, "Will this invoice be paid late: yes or no?" They have years of invoices with the outcome recorded. What type of problem is this?
options: Supervised classification
Supervised regression
Unsupervised clustering
Reinforcement learning
questions.why: The answer is a category (late or not) and past labels exist, so it is supervised classification. It would be regression if the question were "how many days late?", a number; clustering applies only when there is no answer column.

questions.q: Why is part of the data, often 20%, kept aside as a test set that the model never sees in training?
options: To make training faster
Because models can only learn from 80% of the data
To measure generalisation: how well the model predicts new data it has never seen
To give the model extra examples later if accuracy is low
questions.why: Doing well on training data proves nothing; the trainee must be tested on files they never studied. Feeding the test set back in when accuracy disappoints is exactly what destroys its value as an honest check.

questions.q: Four flats: area (hundreds of sq ft) 8, 10, 12, 15; price (₹ lakh) 52, 61, 70, 83. What is the mean squared error of line C: price = 4.5 × area + 15?
questions.why: Predictions 51, 60, 69, 82.5 give errors 1, 1, 1, 0.5; squares 1, 1, 1, 0.25 sum to 3.25; divide by 4: **0.8125**. 3.25 forgets to average; 0.875 averages the plain errors without squaring; 2.25 is line B's MSE. So C beats line B.

questions.q: A churn model is 91% accurate on 500 test customers, of whom 10% actually churned. How should you read this?
options: Excellent: 91% is far above chance
Accuracy cannot be computed when classes are unequal
The model is useless and should be discarded
Predicting "nobody churns" already scores 90%, so the model adds only 1 percentage point of accuracy; look at how many churners it catches
questions.why: Always compare with a simple baseline: 450 of 500 stayed, so the do-nothing model is 90% accurate. Judging 91% against 50% "chance" is the trap. Whether it is useful depends on how many of the 50 churners it finds per customer flagged, so do not discard it on accuracy alone.

questions.q: The fitted line for flat prices is price ≈ 4.43 × area + 16.66, with area in hundreds of sq ft. What does it predict for a 1,300 sq ft flat?
options: About ₹74.3 lakh
About ₹57.6 lakh
About ₹5,776 lakh
About ₹65.4 lakh
questions.why: Area is in hundreds, so use 13: 4.43 × 13 + 16.66 ≈ **₹74.3 lakh**. Plugging in 1,300 directly gives the absurd ₹5,776 lakh (a units slip); ₹57.6 lakh forgets the intercept; ₹65.4 lakh is the prediction for 1,100 sq ft.

questions.q: A price model has training MSE 0.5 and test MSE 40. Predicting the average price for every flat gives a test MSE of 35. What is happening?
options: The model is excellent, because training error is tiny
The test set must be broken, because errors should be similar
The model is overfitting: it memorised the training data and does worse on new data than a simple baseline
The model is underfitting, because test error is high
questions.why: A huge gap between training and test error, with test error worse than a do-nothing baseline, is the signature of overfitting. Underfitting would show high error on both sets. Celebrating the training score is the classic mistake; only performance on unseen data counts.

questions.q: Interview: "When would you advise a client not to use machine learning?" Which answer is best?
options: Never; ML always beats hand-written rules
Whenever the target is a number rather than a category
Only when the data is stored in Excel
When the rules are known and few, the decision is rare, or there is little labelled historical data; a simple rule or a SQL query is cheaper and easier to explain
questions.why: ML pays off when a decision is repeated many times, there is plenty of history with known outcomes, and the rules are too complex to write down. Reaching for ML where a rule would do is a common and costly mistake. Numeric targets are handled by regression, so they are no reason to avoid ML.
